title: Year-to-year temperature responses explain only 2-29% of Chicago bird size declines and not the Amazon or Tanzania trends; the MAPS share is uncertain
abstract: Question: do temporal changes in bird body size follow local warming, as the temperature-size rule predicts? Data: four public CC0 data sets: MAPS banding in North America (105 species, 244,250 adult males, 1989-2018), Chicago window-collision specimens (52 species, 1978-2016), Amazon BDFFP mist nets (43 species, 1979-2019) and Usambara, Tanzania mist nets (21 species, 1987-2022). Method: for each species we measured the observed trend and the slope on the detrended temperature anomaly (CRU TS 4.09 Tmax and Berkeley Earth TAVG). The anomaly slope times the local warming rate gives the trend that warming explains if the long-term response equals the year-to-year response. We controlled station, season, age, sex, capture date, capture hour and bander where the data permit, and pooled species with random effects. Results: in Chicago, warming explains 21-29% of the mass decrease (upper interval 48%) and 2-3% of the tarsus decrease; the wing increase has the opposite sign. In MAPS, mass decreases with temperature, and warming explains 32-43% of the mass decrease, but the bootstrap interval reaches more than 100%. In the Amazon, the sign of the temperature slope depends on the temperature product. In Tanzania, mass increased by 1.3% per decade as the region warmed; the increase is present within one bander's records. In all data sets the trend stays almost the same after the temperature anomaly term. Limitation: a slow long-term response (development, evolution, food) larger than the year-to-year response is not excluded; a MAPS station-warming dose test had no power, and the MAPS extract has no date, time or bander.

display.caption: Observed trait trends (blue) and the trends that local warming implies from the year-to-year temperature response (orange; filled: CRU TS 4.09 Tmax, open: Berkeley Earth TAVG), pooled across species with 95% intervals, in four bird data sets.

Species-level observed mass trends against the mass trends implied by warming (CRU Tmax) in MAPS and Chicago. Points far from the 1:1 line show trends that the temperature response does not explain. Grey bars: 95% intervals of the observed trend.
Usambara, Tanzania: annual mean mass relative to the species-site mean, by bander. Mass increases within the records of bander W.D.N. (1987-2008), so the increase is not only a bander change.

citations.reason: Youngflesh et al. 2022 reported temporal temperature effects on MAPS body size; we test what share of the trend they explain.
Weeks et al. 2020 attributed Chicago size declines to warming; the year-to-year temperature response explains only 2-3% of the tarsus decline and at most about half of the mass decline.
Jirinec et al. 2021 linked Amazon mass declines to climate; our temperature slope sign depends on the temperature product.
Usambara morphometric data with bander identity (CC0).
Neate-Clegg et al. 2023 reported Afromontane mass increases; the increase is present within one bander's records.
Probst et al. 2026 found relative mass declines that temperature did not predict; we find that temperature responses explain a minority of trends.
